title: Leading a band at Pete Herman's
summary: He led a five-piece band at Pete Herman's, hired Charlie Stowe, left for the shipyard, then took the St. Charles Theater job.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: When did you go into Pete Herman's?

Well, the first, I worked at Pete Herman three different times. The first time when I went to New York he wanted me to put a band in his place and I told him I was all set to go to New York. But when I came back, 1940, I had a band in Pete Herman's and when the war came out I left to go to work in a shipyard. I left Pete Herman's. And I did him a very nice favor by putting all four F-men on the job and left. You know, fellas that wouldn't be called into the draft. Like Irwin Dennis who weighed almost 300 pounds, they didn't want him, you know.
Yeah, and the drummer's still there incidentally. Who's that?

He's still working at Pete Herman's. It's 17 or 18 years now. His only job, his first union job. And when I hired him I put him in the union and he said, you think this job would be steady? I said, well I think so. I mean I couldn't guarantee him but it seems the story turned out to be steady, huh? Eighteen years. Yeah.
Who was in the band there then when you first started, Pete Herman?

Well I had five men. I had Louis Escobedo, at that time I had Bob Doyle on piano, and Charlie Stowe, and I had a bass player by the name of Lonnie Mitchell from Texas, who later was replaced by Johnny Bell. Remember Johnny Bell? You probably heard of him. He played bass. He died some years ago. But a nice little group, five pieces. Then Louis left, Louis Escobedo left, and I got Bill McElhaney. Bill's playing at WSM in Nashville. He's the staff arranger. Very fine trumpet player. Then Pete Herman closed for remodeling so I didn't go back. It took too long to come back so Fazola organized the band and I went with him. Four saxes and three or four brass, a big band, you know, and we waited for quite a while. And then Fazola saw the end in sight for the job so he tipped me off. He says, I don't think we would be on this job too much longer. The business looks pretty bad so that's all I needed was a little hint. So I accepted the job at the St. Charles Theater and incidentally played every chair in the sax section. I started on fourth tenor, moved to second tenor, and then moved to third alto and ended up playing lead alto. I worked there three years and then from there I went back to the 500 Club.
